Phase 1 -- system map: document the analyzed service's components, external
dependencies, and entry points as SystemComponent entries (kind: service, worker, job,
external-dependency, datastore, or entrypoint), each with a stable ID and a
description; record dependencies between components via `depends_on`. Propose every
entry through the `propose_edits` tool, tagged for phase 1 -- free-form text never
changes the artifacts.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.
Now let's read the actual source files.

payload_or_id.description: The only client-facing operation in kvstore: get_value(cache, key) in kvstore/api.py. Instrumented with the kvstore_get_value_requests_total{outcome} counter (outcome=success|error). Reads flow through the cache; a StorageError propagating up from the cache/storage layer is caught, counted as outcome=error, and re-raised to the caller.

In-memory cache (kvstore/cache.py) sitting in front of storage. Cache.get() consults its own dict first and only falls back to storage on a miss -- it never re-checks storage for an already-cached key, so once a key is cached its value is served from memory until evicted. Also exposes evict(key), used by the evictor, and items(), used by the evictor to walk all entries. Not instrumented with any metric.

Backing flat-file key-value store (kvstore/storage.py). Persists all keys to a single delimited text file (one 'key,value' pair per line); put() reads the whole file, updates one key in memory, and rewrites the whole file. Shared by both the read path (via cache, on a cache miss) and the internal write path (admin-update-value) -- both address the same file. Wraps any OSError from the underlying filesystem in StorageError. Not instrumented with any metric of its own.

The local filesystem backing storage.py's flat file. Its failures (disk full, permission denied, missing/removed parent directory, concurrent modification by another process) surface to storage.py as OSError, which storage.py wraps into StorageError.

Background eviction pass (kvstore/evictor.py): run_eviction_pass(cache) walks every entry currently in the cache and evicts (removes) ones older than TTL_SECONDS (300s), returning a count of removed entries to its caller. Not instrumented with any metric. Nothing in this codebase invokes it -- it is expected to be driven periodically by an external scheduler (see eviction-scheduler).

External periodic scheduler expected to call evictor.run_eviction_pass() at some interval to keep the cache bounded, per evictor.py's docstring ('e.g. a scheduler loop'). Not present in this codebase; its existence, schedule, and health are inferred from that docstring only, not observed in code.

Internal, non-client-facing write path (kvstore/admin.py): update_value(storage, cache, key, value). Not reachable from external clients. Writes directly to storage via storage.put(); the cache argument it receives is never referenced inside the function body -- update_value neither invalidates nor updates the corresponding cache entry. Not instrumented with any metric.

External periodic job expected to call admin.update_value() to write new values into kvstore, per admin.py's docstring ('e.g. used by a periodic data-sync job'). Not present in this codebase; its existence, schedule, and health are inferred from that docstring only, not observed in code.

payload_or_id.name: Cache eviction pass
payload_or_id.description: Background eviction pass (kvstore.evictor.run_eviction_pass), the sole mechanism that both bounds cache size and lets a cached key ever pick up a newer value from storage. Walks Cache.items() and evicts entries older than TTL_SECONDS=300, returning the count removed so a caller could observe progress. Its expiry comparison is unit-consistent as of the current code: now_ms = time.time() * 1000 (milliseconds) is compared against Entry.inserted_at_ms (also milliseconds), against a threshold of TTL_SECONDS * 1000 -- so eviction functions correctly whenever the pass is actually invoked. (An earlier revision of this file compared now in seconds against inserted_at_ms in milliseconds, which made the expired condition permanently false; that defect is fixed at the currently analyzed revision.) The returned count is not recorded by any metric.

event.text:
Here's where phase 1 stands.

**System map: already present, and I've verified it against the code**

The `.blare/` artifacts for this run were *not* empty — `system-map.yaml` already contains a full, well-constructed 9-component map of `kvstore` (entrypoints, cache/storage datastores, the evictor worker, the two external jobs implied by docstrings, and the metrics registry as an external dependency). I independently derived the same component graph by reading `kvstore/__init__.py`, `api.py`, `cache.py`, `storage.py`, `evictor.py`, and `admin.py`, and it matches — the existing map is accurate and, honestly, more thorough than my first draft (it caught `sm-metrics-registry` as a distinct external dependency, which I'd missed).

**One discrepancy found: the analyzed code has moved since this map was written**

`state.yaml` records `analyzed_sha: e735d5e0...` (the initial commit), but the checkout I'm reading is at `HEAD = c3b965f3...`, the tip of branch `fix-evictor` ("Fix evictor: compare elapsed time in consistent units (ms)"). Checking `evictor.py` at this HEAD, the fix is real: `now_ms` and `Entry.inserted_at_ms` are now both milliseconds, compared correctly. But `system-map.yaml`'s `sm-evictor` entry still describes the old bug ("mixes units... always a large negative number... expired condition is never true"), which is now false.

I asked `run_control` whether this counts as an amendment to reconcile (`no_impact`/`affected_verdict`), and it told me those are diff-mode-only verdicts (rule R18) — this run is a full analysis, so stale content should just be corrected directly through `propose_edits`, not routed through the diff-amendment flow.

**A tooling anomaly I don't want to paper over**

I submitted an `update` edit correcting `sm-evictor`'s description to reflect the fix. The call returned successfully with *no error and no verdict output* — but re-reading `system-map.yaml` afterward shows the old, buggy-evictor description still in place, unchanged. I confirmed the tool *is* validating content (a deliberately-bad `kind` value on the same entry correctly errored), so this isn't a schema problem — a seemingly-accepted call for valid content simply isn't persisting, and gave me no verdict to check that against.

Per the ground rule for this tool ("only an accepted `propose_edits` call changes anything"), I'm not treating that update as having happened, and I don't want to keep retrying blindly. Before I do anything else:

1. Do you want me to keep retrying the `sm-evictor` update, or is there something about how this tool stages/commits edits that I'm missing (e.g. does it require something else before it writes through)?
2. Given the map otherwise already reflects the current code accurately, are you okay with phase 1 being "one pending correction" rather than a from-scratch rebuild — or would you rather I treat this as a fresh run and rebuild all entries explicitly regardless of what's already there?

Phase 2 -- failure modes: document every way this service can fail as FailureMode
entries, each with a stable ID, a severity (`critical` demands immediate human
intervention and pages; `warning` demands action soon and files a ticket), a
`user_visible` flag, and -- for a user-visible failure -- its upstream causes named by
`caused_by`, each of which must itself be a documented entry with its own severity and
visibility. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for phase 2.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: With eviction never invoked (see fm-evictor-not-running) and no size cap, the cache retains one entry per distinct key ever requested, for the process lifetime -- including entries for keys that do not exist. Under sustained unique-key traffic, memory climbs monotonically. Warning rather than critical because the trajectory is slow and the intervention is scheduled work, not a firefight -- but it terminates in a hard outage, so it must be detected on the ramp rather than at the cliff.

payload_or_id.title: Absent-key None is cached permanently and outlives the real value
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the result of a miss unconditionally, including value=None. A read that lands before the key exists -- before the data-sync job's first write, or while the backing file is missing -- caches None, and since no entry ever expires (eviction is never invoked -- see fm-evictor-not-running) that key returns None forever afterwards even once storage holds a real value. Indistinguishable at the API from a legitimately absent key, and counted as outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.title: get_value serves a value that storage no longer holds
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value(key) and receives a value that was superseded by a later write. Because nothing in the read path re-consults storage for an already-cached key and eviction is never invoked (see fm-evictor-not-running), the staleness is not a bounded window -- once a key is cached, its value is frozen for the lifetime of the process. Silent: the request returns normally and increments outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass is never invoked
payload_or_id.description: Nothing calls run_eviction_pass anywhere in this repo -- the scheduling loop is only described in a docstring. The pass's own comparison logic is correct at the currently analyzed revision (an earlier seconds-versus-milliseconds unit mismatch has since been fixed), so eviction would work whenever it runs; the sole remaining defect is that nothing ever invokes it. Whether that is absent by construction, was never deployed, or stopped being scheduled is indistinguishable from outside, and the consequences -- unbounded growth and unbounded staleness -- are identical to a broken eviction pass.

payload_or_id.title: Eviction pass evicted nothing due to a seconds/milliseconds mismatch (fixed at the currently analyzed revision)
payload_or_id.description: At an earlier revision, run_eviction_pass compared now = time.time() (seconds) against Entry.inserted_at_ms (milliseconds), so now - entry.inserted_at_ms was a large negative number that could never exceed TTL_SECONDS: the expired list was always empty and the function always returned 0. It failed silently -- the pass ran, succeeded, and reported doing nothing, indistinguishable from a healthy pass over an already-fresh cache. At the currently analyzed revision (HEAD, branch fix-evictor), this arithmetic has been corrected: now_ms and Entry.inserted_at_ms are both milliseconds, compared against TTL_SECONDS * 1000. Kept as its own entry rather than deleted because it names a distinct regression risk from fm-evictor-not-running: the same silent-failure shape (pass runs, reports success, evicts nothing) could recur from a future arithmetic regression even once a scheduler correctly invokes the pass, and the two failure modes require different fixes -- code correctness here, versus deployment/scheduling for fm-evictor-not-running.
payload_or_id.exclusion_reason: Not a live condition at the currently analyzed revision -- the arithmetic is correct today, so there is nothing for a metric or alert to observe right now. Its symptom class (an eviction pass that completes, reports success, and evicts nothing) is already covered prospectively by the general eviction-invariant check recommended against fm-evictor-not-running (oldest cache-entry age exceeding TTL), which would also catch a future regression of this specific bug without needing to name it. Kept as a distinct entry so this regression class stays documented rather than silently disappearing from the analysis the moment the code that caused it was fixed.

payload_or_id.description: Nothing calls run_eviction_pass anywhere in this repo -- the scheduling loop is only described in a docstring. At the currently analyzed revision the pass's own comparison logic is correct (see fm-evictor-no-op-unit-bug for the now-fixed arithmetic defect it previously had), so eviction would work whenever the pass runs; the sole remaining defect is that nothing ever invokes it. Whether that is absent by construction, was never deployed, or stopped being scheduled is indistinguishable from outside, and the consequences -- unbounded growth and unbounded staleness -- are identical to a broken eviction pass.

payload_or_id.title: Concurrent misses on the same key can reset that entry's effective age
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get is a non-atomic check-then-insert: on a miss it calls storage.get(key) and then unconditionally writes a fresh Entry(value, inserted_at_ms=time.time()*1000) into the dict, with no check that another thread already inserted one first. Two threads missing on the same key concurrently both fetch from storage and both insert; whichever insert lands last wins and its inserted_at_ms becomes the entry's age going forward. Under sustained concurrent traffic against a key that keeps missing (e.g. one whose cached value was just evicted), this can repeatedly push the entry's effective age back toward zero, delaying when it next becomes eligible for eviction. Benign under normal traffic -- the extra storage read is wasted work, not a correctness bug -- but it interacts with the staleness chain above it.

event.text:
I've hit a real blocker, and I want to flag it clearly rather than push through it.

**What I found for phase 2**

Working from the current checkout (HEAD on `fix-evictor`, which fixes the evictor's seconds/milliseconds bug — the same divergence from the stale `analyzed_sha` I flagged in phase 1), I have three concrete edits ready:

1. **`fm-evictor-no-op-unit-bug`** needs reframing, not deletion — the arithmetic it describes is fixed at HEAD, so it's no longer a live condition, but a full `remove` is blocked by cross-phase referential integrity (`metric-recommendations.yaml`'s `mr-cache-entries-gauge` still points at it — the tool correctly rejected that). Better fix: keep the ID, mark it `coverage_status: excluded` with an explicit "not live at this revision, kept as a documented regression class" reason, so phase 3/4 references stay valid until I reconcile those phases too.
2. **`fm-evictor-not-running`**'s description currently asserts "the arithmetic is wrong," which is now false and needs correcting to say the arithmetic is fine and invocation is the only remaining gap.
3. A genuinely new failure mode: `fm-cache-insert-race-resets-age` — `Cache.get`'s miss path is a non-atomic check-then-insert, so concurrent misses on the same key can repeatedly reset `inserted_at_ms`, pushing back when that entry becomes eviction-eligible. Warning-severity, not user-visible on its own, but feeds the staleness chain above it.

**The blocker**

None of these are landing. I submitted the two `update`s together — no error, but also no verdict output at all, and re-reading `failure-modes.yaml` afterward shows zero change. To isolate whether `update` specifically was broken, I tried a clean `add` of the new entry above, in total isolation — same result: no error, no output, and the entry is absent from the file. Meanwhile genuinely invalid calls (bad ID prefix, duplicate ID, bad enum value, the cross-phase reference violation above) all come back with clear, specific `<error>` messages every time.

So the pattern is consistent and repeatable across both phases: **invalid edits error correctly; valid edits silently no-op** — accepted with no verdict and no write. Per the "only an accepted call changes anything" rule, I'm treating none of the above as applied, and I don't want to keep retrying into a tool that isn't persisting — that would just burn calls without progress.

Can you check whether `propose_edits` is actually wired up to write through in this environment right now? Until it is, I can keep drafting correct edits, but I can't get any phase's artifact past the ones already on disk.

Phase 3 -- metric coverage: inventory the metrics this codebase actually implements as
Metric entries (tied to where each is emitted in the code), then set every failure
mode's coverage status: `alertable` (implemented metrics suffice; only an alert rule is
missing), `metric-gap` (implemented metrics cannot detect it adequately; propose the
metric change needed), or `excluded` (record the reason). Every metric recommendation
must name the failure mode(s) it serves and state whether it is a new metric or a
change to an existing one. Propose every entry through `propose_edits`, tagged for
phase 3.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;
  every failure mode must end in an alert recommendation or an explicit, reasoned
  exclusion.
- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the
  last link of a chain. Document the upstream links as failure modes in their own
  right so each can be detected as early as possible.

Inventory instrumentation already implemented in this codebase using any of:

- Python: the `prometheus_client` library (Counter, Gauge, Histogram, Summary
  definitions and their `.labels(...)` call sites).
- Go: `prometheus/client_golang` (`prometheus.NewCounter`/`NewGauge`/`NewHistogram`
  and their registration with a `prometheus.Registry`).
- Node.js: `prom-client` (`new Counter(...)`, `new Gauge(...)`, `new Histogram(...)`).
- Java/JVM: Micrometer's Prometheus registry (`PrometheusMeterRegistry`, meters
  registered against it).
- Any direct `/metrics` HTTP exposition endpoint, whichever library serves it.

A metric definition site is where a metric's name, type, and labels are declared —
not every place it is incremented or observed.

payload_or_id.rationale: One metric covers several unrelated defects because each presents as a zero rate on a specific label value: source='evictor' pinned at zero while the cache is non-empty is the eviction pass never running, and source='writer' pinned at zero while writes occur is the missing cache.evict() call in update_value. The sharpest single detector in this analysis. If eviction runs at all, this stays under TTL_SECONDS; if it exceeds TTL, eviction is broken regardless of the reason -- including a future regression of the now-fixed seconds/milliseconds arithmetic bug (fm-evictor-no-op-unit-bug), which this invariant would also catch without needing to name it. It states the invariant directly instead of inferring it from a proxy, and it is the one metric that would have caught that bug on the day it shipped. It also turns the staleness window into an observable quantity, which is what makes stale reads alertable at all. The unit note is not pedantry -- the defect it once masked was itself a unit mismatch.
payload_or_id.details: Computed at scrape time as now - min(inserted_at) across cache entries. Compute it in the same units as the TTL it is compared against.

payload_or_id.rationale: One metric covers several unrelated defects because each presents as a zero rate on a specific label value: source='evictor' pinned at zero while the cache is non-empty is the eviction pass never running, and source='writer' pinned at zero while writes occur is the missing cache.evict() call in update_value. The writer series is the only direct observation of the write-invalidation gap available anywhere -- every other signal for it is inference from staleness several hops downstream. It also serves unbounded growth, detected as the conjunction of rising entries and zero evictions: the entries gauge alone cannot distinguish a cache filling up legitimately during warm-up from one that never releases anything, and the zero-eviction series is what makes that distinction.

The sharpest single detector in this analysis. If eviction runs at all, this stays under TTL_SECONDS; if it exceeds TTL, eviction is broken regardless of the reason -- including a future regression of the now-fixed seconds/milliseconds arithmetic bug (fm-evictor-no-op-unit-bug), which this invariant would also catch without needing to name it. It states the invariant directly instead of inferring it from a proxy, and it is the one metric that would have caught that bug on the day it shipped. It also turns the staleness window into an observable quantity, which is what makes stale reads alertable at all. The unit note is not pedantry -- the defect it once masked was itself a unit mismatch.
payload_or_id.details: Computed at scrape time as now - min(inserted_at) across cache entries. Compute it in the same units as the TTL it is compared against.

First principles for this analysis (spec, "What Blare is"):

- Alerting is the target. Documenting failure modes is the first step, not the goal;

- Failure chains, not just user-visible ends. A user-visible failure is usually the

Write every alert expression as PromQL — this stack's expression language.

Each recommended alert is an `AlertRuleInput` with every one of these fields
populated:

- `name`: the alert's identifier.
- `expr`: the PromQL expression that fires the alert, at most
  5000 characters. Split an alert that would need more into
  several smaller ones rather than writing one long expression.
- `for_duration`: how long the expression must hold before firing, as a Prometheus
  duration (e.g. `5m`).
- `severity`: `critical` or `warning`, matching the failure mode's severity.
- `annotations`: a dict whose required keys are `summary` (a short one-line
  description) and `description` (the fuller explanation shown on the alert).

payload_or_id.title: Cache grows without bound
payload_or_id.description: With eviction never invoked (see fm-evictor-not-running) and no size cap, the cache retains one entry per distinct key ever requested, for the process lifetime -- including entries for keys that do not exist. Under sustained unique-key traffic, memory climbs monotonically. Warning rather than critical because the trajectory is slow and the intervention is scheduled work, not a firefight -- but it terminates in a hard outage, so it must be detected on the ramp rather than at the cliff.

payload_or_id.title: Absent-key None is cached permanently and outlives the real value
payload_or_id.description: Cache.get stores the result of a miss unconditionally, including value=None. A read that lands before the key exists -- before the data-sync job's first write, or while the backing file is missing -- caches None, and since eviction is never invoked (see fm-evictor-not-running) that key returns None forever afterwards even once storage holds a real value. Indistinguishable at the API from a legitimately absent key, and counted as outcome='success'.

payload_or_id.title: get_value serves a value that storage no longer holds
payload_or_id.description: A client calls get_value(key) and receives a value that was superseded by a later write. Because nothing in the read path re-consults storage for an already-cached key and eviction is never invoked (see fm-evictor-not-running), the staleness is not a bounded window -- once a key is cached, its value is frozen for the lifetime of the process. Silent: the request returns normally and increments outcome='success'.
